title: C# and Unity in a solution
sub: struct versus class, dictionary keys, Span and ArrayPool, hidden allocations, recursion depth and the Boehm GC
cards/0/title: struct or class: nodes and pairs
cards/0/body:
A class is a reference type: an object on the managed heap (on 64-bit, a 16-byte header plus the fields), the variable holds a reference, and assignment copies the reference. A struct is a value type: the data lives right in the variable, field or array slot, and assignment or passing to a method copies the whole value.

Hence the rule for interview problems. Small data — a cell, a “distance and vertex” pair, a segment — should be a readonly struct: a Cell[] array is contiguous in memory, with no separate object per element and no work for the GC. Nodes that point at each other (a tree, a list, a graph) are a class: a struct cannot hold a field of its own type. Or skip objects altogether and use indices into arrays: int[] left, right instead of references.

The copy trap: if the struct is mutable, var c = cells[i]; c.X++; changes a copy, and the array element stays as it was. With a List<Cell>, list[i].X = 5 does not even compile: the indexer returns a copy. That is why structs in solutions are made immutable.
cards/1/title: Dictionary keys: IEquatable, tuples and boxing
cards/1/body:
Dictionary and HashSet compare keys through EqualityComparer<T>.Default. If the struct implements IEquatable<T>, its Equals(T) is called directly. If not, it is Equals(object), and the key gets boxed: a copy of the struct goes to the heap as an object, on every comparison. On top of that, the default ValueType.Equals and GetHashCode are slow and may not hash every field. The result is garbage on every lookup and a poor spread across buckets.

Three good keys for a grid cell:

1. The tuple (int x, int y): ValueTuple already implements IEquatable and a decent GetHashCode. The shortest option with no boxing.
2. Your own struct with IEquatable<Cell> and GetHashCode via HashCode.Combine.
3. A single number: y * width + x as an int or ((long)x << 32) | (uint)y as a long. This is the fastest, and if the grid size is known you need no dictionary at all — a bool[width * height] will do.

Bad keys: Tuple<int, int> (a class — an object per key) and the string $"{x},{y}" (a new string and format parsing on every lookup).
cards/2/q: Which keys for a HashSet of visited cells create no garbage on every lookup? Select all.
cards/2/explain: A tuple and a struct with IEquatable are compared through Equals(T) without boxing, and an int is just a number. A struct without IEquatable goes through Equals(object) and is boxed on every comparison. Tuple<int, int> is a class: an object for every key you create. A string is a new string on every lookup.
cards/3/title: Span<T> and stackalloc: counters off the heap
cards/3/body:
stackalloc allocates an array on the stack of the current method: the memory is released on return, the GC does not know about it, and nothing is allocated on the heap. With Span<T> it is safe code, no unsafe needed: Span<int> counts = stackalloc int[26]; is a letter counter for zero bytes of garbage.

Span<T> is a window onto contiguous memory: an array, a slice of one, a string (ReadOnlySpan<char>), the stack. Slice and AsSpan do not copy: s.AsSpan(1, 3) instead of s.Substring(1, 3) — no new string.

Limits. The stack is small (typically 1 MB per thread), so stackalloc is only for small sizes known in advance: 26 letters, 256 bytes, 64 neighbours; for an n that comes from the input, use a pool, covered next. Span is a ref struct: it cannot go into a class field, be captured by a lambda, or live across await or yield. The documentation treats the contents of stackalloc memory as undefined: if you need zeros, call Clear(). Unity has Span since 2021.2.
cards/4/title: ArrayPool<T>: a large buffer without garbage
cards/4/body:
When you need a buffer of input size n (10⁵–10⁶ elements), and often at that — once a frame or per request — new int[n] every time produces a lot of garbage. ArrayPool<T>.Shared hands arrays out again and again, and it comes with three rules:

1. Rent(n) returns an array of length at least n (usually rounded up to a power of two) — work with the first n elements, not with Length. In Unity (as in .NET before 6) the shared pool only keeps arrays of up to 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 elements: a larger Rent allocates a new array every time.
2. The array is not cleared: it holds the previous owner’s data. If you need zeros, use Array.Clear or Fill.
3. Return goes in finally; after returning, do not touch the array and never return it twice.

A common pairing: small size — stackalloc, large — the pool. Unity has ArrayPool (.NET Standard 2.1), but in an interview the simpler answer is often “a buffer in a class field, reused every frame” — also zero allocations, and no rental rules.
cards/5/body:
Code without a single new can still produce garbage. What allocates on the heap:

LINQ. Where, Select, OrderBy create iterator objects, ToList and ToArray create new collections, and OrderBy also copies the data and costs O(n log n) where a single pass would do.
Closures. A lambda that captures a local variable creates, on every call of the method, a closure object for the captured state and a new delegate; if it captures only this, it is one new delegate. A lambda without captures is cached by the compiler and does not allocate.
params. Log(params object[] args) is a new array per call, and every number in it is boxed as well.
Strings. +, Substring, ToString, interpolation — a new string; s += x in a loop is O(n²) copying, use a StringBuilder instead. In C# 9 (Unity), $"{hp}" with a number goes through string.Format and boxes hp.
Boxing. A struct converted to object or to an interface is copied to the heap. The sneakiest case is foreach over an interface. The enumerator of List<T> is a struct, and foreach over the List<T> itself creates no garbage. But foreach over a variable of type IEnumerable<T> gets the enumerator through the interface — boxed.
Iterators. A method with yield return is an object per call.
cards/5/code:
var alive = enemies.Where(e => e.Hp > 0).ToList(); // an iterator and a new list
int limit = 10;
enemies.Find(e => e.Hp < limit);    // captures limit: an object and a delegate per call
string s = "HP: " + hp;             // a new string
Debug.LogFormat("{0} {1}", x, y);   // params object[] and boxing of x, y
IEnumerable<Enemy> seq = enemies;
foreach (var e in seq) { }          // enumerator through the interface — boxed
foreach (var e in enemies) { }      // List<T>.Enumerator is a struct, 0 B
cards/5/deep:
Delegates from methods. Before C# 11, list.Find(IsAlive) creates a new delegate on every method group conversion, even for a static method. C# 11 caches the delegate for a static method, but Unity is C# 9: keep the delegate in a static readonly field. The static modifier on a lambda (C# 9) forbids captures at compile time — a handy safety net.

Unity APIs that return new arrays. Physics.RaycastAll and OverlapSphere return a new array on every call; RaycastNonAlloc and OverlapSphereNonAlloc write into your buffer. GetComponents<T>() is a new array, while the GetComponents(List<T>) overload fills the list you pass. gameObject.tag == "Enemy" creates a string, CompareTag("Enemy") does not.

How to find them. The Profiler’s GC Alloc column, plus Deep Profile mode to see the call that allocates. In .NET, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() before and after a piece of code, and BenchmarkDotNet with [MemoryDiagnoser] in performance tests.
cards/6/q: This Update runs every frame; seen is a HashSet<(int, int)> field, enemies is a List<Enemy>. One line creates heap garbage on every call. Tap it.
cards/6/explain: foreach over a variable of type IEnumerable<Enemy> calls GetEnumerator through the interface, and the List<Enemy>.Enumerator struct gets boxed — an object every frame. Everything else is clean: Clear keeps the capacity, stackalloc is the stack, the tuple is a value, and foreach over the List<T> itself uses the struct enumerator. HashSet.Add allocates only when the set runs out of capacity — after the first few frames it has enough.
cards/7/body:
Every method call pushes a frame onto the thread stack: the return address, arguments, local variables — tens or hundreds of bytes. The stack is small: typically 1 MB per thread on Windows, sometimes more on other platforms, but of the same order. A depth of thousands or tens of thousands of calls is fine; a million is not.

Where it bites: a recursive depth-first search over a 1000×1000 grid. If the whole map is solid land or one long snaking corridor, the depth reaches 10⁶. That is a StackOverflowException, and in .NET it cannot be caught: try/catch will not help, the process terminates. In Unity it varies: Mono in the editor sometimes manages to throw it into the console, while an IL2CPP build usually just crashes — you cannot rely on catch anywhere. C# does not promise to turn tail recursion into a loop.

The cure is an explicit stack: a Stack<T> on the heap instead of the call stack. The memory is the same, O(n) in the worst case, but the heap is large, and the traversal order stays depth-first. If order does not matter (flood fill, counting islands), a Queue<T> works too — breadth-first search. In an interview, say it out loud: “recursion is shorter, but for 10⁶ cells I would use an explicit stack”.
cards/8/q: A Unity game counts islands on a 2000×2000 map with a recursive depth-first search. On a 100×100 test map everything worked. What happens on the big map, where almost everything is land?
cards/8/options/0: The stack overflows both on Mono in the editor and in an IL2CPP build: the build crashes, and a try/catch around the call is no protection
cards/8/options/1: In the editor on Mono the stack overflows, but an IL2CPP build finishes: native C++ code uses less stack per call
cards/8/options/2: An IL2CPP build throws a StackOverflowException — we catch it and switch to breadth-first search
cards/8/options/3: Both Mono and IL2CPP turn the recursion into a loop when compiling — the traversal finishes, just slower than on 100×100
cards/8/explain: On solid land the recursion depth reaches 4·10⁶ calls, while the stack is on the order of a megabyte. That overflows on any runtime: a StackOverflowException cannot be caught in .NET, the process terminates; Mono in the editor sometimes manages to show it in the console, but an IL2CPP build crashes. Time has nothing to do with it — the stack memory runs out. The way out is an explicit Stack<T> or a breadth-first search with a Queue<T>.
cards/8/wrong/1: Even at 32 bytes per frame, 4·10⁶ calls take 128 MB, while a thread stack is on the order of a megabyte, native code included. The IL2CPP build crashes just the same — only without a message in the console.
cards/8/wrong/2: A stack overflow cannot be caught: in .NET the process terminates before control reaches the catch, and an IL2CPP build simply crashes. An explicit stack or a breadth-first search is chosen up front, not after the crash.
cards/8/wrong/3: C# does not promise to turn recursion into a loop on any runtime, and here there is nothing to turn: after a call returns, three more follow — this is not tail recursion. The depth stays at 4·10⁶ frames.
cards/9/title: GC in Unity: Boehm and “0 B per frame”
cards/9/body:
Unity runs the Boehm–Demers–Weiser collector on both Mono and IL2CPP. How it differs from the .NET (CoreCLR) collector:

No generations. In .NET short-lived garbage is cheap: the young generation is collected quickly and often. Boehm marks the entire managed heap every time, so the cost of a collection grows with the heap size, not with the amount of garbage.
No compaction. Objects do not move: the heap fragments, grows, and rarely gives memory back to the OS.
Stops the world. While marking runs, scripts wait. Incremental mode (on by default in Player Settings) slices the marking across frames: the spike is smaller, but the total work is the same, plus the cost of write barriers.

Hence the norm: code that runs every frame allocates 0 bytes — the GC Alloc column in the Profiler. How to get there: collections and buffers in fields, Clear() instead of new, capacity up front, object pools, structs, no LINQ and no closures in Update. One-off allocations while a level loads are fine.
cards/9/deep:
Conservativeness. Boehm scans stacks conservatively: any machine word that looks like an object’s address keeps that object alive. So a “dead” object sometimes survives a collection — correctness is unaffected, but memory can be held longer than you expect.

Control from code. UnityEngine.Scripting.GarbageCollector.GCMode lets you switch collection off during a fight and back on at a loading screen — only if the fight allocates almost nothing, otherwise the heap grows without bound. GarbageCollector.incrementalTimeSliceNanoseconds sets the per-frame slice of incremental collection. An explicit GC.Collect() belongs to pauses and scene changes, not to the game loop.

Compared with .NET. In CoreCLR an object in generation 0 that dies before a collection costs almost nothing: the collector copies only the survivors. So “do not allocate” on a server is about throughput, while in Unity it is about frame spikes. In an interview it is worth saying why the rule is stricter in Unity.
cards/10/title: NativeArray, Jobs and Burst: when they fit
cards/10/body:
When there really is a lot of data — thousands of agents, a direction field on a 512×512 grid (262,144 cells), hundreds of path searches per frame — Unity has a route around the managed heap. NativeArray<T> is memory outside the GC, and its elements must be unmanaged structs. Jobs spread work across cores (IJobParallelFor splits a range of indices). Burst compiles such a job into vectorized machine code and gives a several-fold speed-up.

The price: manual Dispose() (or a leak that the editor will warn about), allocators (Temp — within a frame, TempJob — up to four frames, Persistent — as long as needed), and no classes, strings or managed arrays inside a job.

In an interview you write the algorithm on plain arrays first. Jobs and Burst answer the question “what if there are 10,000 units?”: “the data goes into a NativeArray, the traversal into a Burst job, and I read the result next frame”. Dragging them into a whiteboard solution when nobody asked is overkill.
cards/11/title: C# 9 in Unity: what is missing
cards/11/body:
Unity compiles scripts as C# 9. Newer syntax that feels natural after .NET 8 will not compile in a Unity interview:

C# 10: record struct, file-scoped namespace X;, global using, interpolated strings without boxing.
C# 11: the unsigned shift >>> (in C# 9, (int)((uint)x >> k)), list patterns is [var first, ..], raw strings """, required, generic math (static abstract in interfaces), cached delegates for static methods.
C# 12: collection expressions int[] a = [1, 2, 3]; (in C# 9, new[] { 1, 2, 3 }), primary constructors on classes.

What C# 9 does have: target-typed new(), is not null, and and or in patterns, switch expressions, static lambdas, tuples, local functions. init properties and positional record types only work if you declare an empty System.Runtime.CompilerServices.IsExternalInit class in the project — the Unity profile does not have it.
cards/12/q: Match the situation with the technique.
cards/12/pairs/1/1: An array in a field, or ArrayPool
cards/12/pairs/2/0: A grid cell key in a HashSet
cards/12/pairs/3/1: An explicit Stack<T> instead of recursion
cards/12/pairs/5/0: A tree node with references to children
cards/12/pairs/5/1: A class, or indices into arrays
